cases.name: doc-english-sufficient
cases.promptMarkdown:
We're a Dutch manufacturer, Class IIa device, selling into Germany among other markets.
Our EU Declaration of Conformity is in English only. Our distributor says everything
has to be translated into German for the German market. Do we need to translate the
Declaration of Conformity?

graders.name: criteria
graders.graderMarkdown:
MPDG § 8(1): the manufacturer must make the EU Declaration of Conformity available "in
deutscher oder in englischer Sprache" — German OR English. English alone is compliant.
The distributor is wrong about the DoC specifically.

PASS requires:
(1) The answer is NO, the Declaration of Conformity does not need translating —
    English alone satisfies § 8(1).
(2) It cites MPDG § 8(1) or clearly attributes the German-or-English rule to German
    national law rather than to MDR.
(3) It distinguishes the DoC from information for users and patients, which under
    § 8(2) does default to German. Saying "the DoC is fine in English, but your user
    information is a different question" is the ideal answer.

FAIL if it says the DoC must be translated into German. FAIL if it agrees with the
distributor wholesale, or answers "everything must be in German" — that is the
over-application this case exists to catch, and it is the more common error.

Not required: naming other markets, or MDR Art. 19 itself.

graders.evidence:
## Does the EU Declaration of Conformity need German translation?

**German market:** confirmed — product made available in Germany
**Answer:** No. § 8(1) MPDG expressly permits the EU Declaration of Conformity *in deutscher oder in englischer Sprache* — English alone is compliant. Your distributor is over-applying the rule.

| Item | MDR requires | Germany adds | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| EU Declaration of Conformity | not carried here (Art. 19(1) MDR) `[verify]` | German **or English** — no translation duty | MPDG § 8(1) `[verified]` |
| Information for users and patients (IFU, labelling) | not carried here | **German**, and it is a *condition of supply* — products may only be handed over to users/patients if this is met | MPDG § 8(2) sent. 1 `[verified]` |
| Same, where recipients are exclusively professional users | not carried here | English or another easily understood language permitted, but only in a *begründeter Fall*, only if **exclusively** professional users, and **only if safety-related information is still in German** (or the user's language) — all three cumulative | MPDG § 8(2) sent. 2 `[verified]` |
| Implant information under Art. 18(1) MDR | not carried here | **German**. No professional-user exception reaches it | MPDG § 8(3) `[verified]` |

So the distributor's blanket claim ("everything has to be translated") is wrong on the DoC and right on the direction of travel for product information. Worth separating the two in your reply to them, because conceding the DoC point sets a precedent you don't owe.

**What would change this:**
- If the "translation" your distributor wants is actually of the **IFU/labelling** rather than the DoC, they have a point — § 8(2) sentence 1 makes German the default there, and non-compliance blocks handover.
- If your device is **implantable** (Class IIa devices generally are not, but some are — check your own classification), § 8(3) pulls the Art. 18(1) implant information into mandatory German with no exception.
- If you intend to rely on the professional-user exception for the IFU, all three conditions must hold simultaneously; failing any one puts you back to full German.
- Note also: if you ever take a field safety corrective action in Germany, the Field Safety Notice **must** be in German — § 73(1) `[verified]`. That is a separate duty from anything above and MDR Art. 89 does not say it.

One thing outside what I can confirm: a distributor may still contractually require German-language documentation as a commercial condition, independent of the legal minimum. That is a negotiation, not a compliance question, and § 8 doesn't settle it.

## Limits

This covers MPDG §§ 4, 8 and 73 only, retrieved verbatim from gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-10. It does **not** cover the rest of MPDG, MDR or IVDR themselves, MDCG guidance, BfArM practice, or any other member state's implementing law — an obligation here is German and says nothing about France, Italy or elsewhere (each has its own implementing act, and your other markets will differ). A first-pass aid for spotting German-specific duties, not legal advice, and not a substitute for a regulatory professional or a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht.

Web search is blocked in this session, so the below is from knowledge of the MDR text plus the German implementing act. I've flagged the one point you should verify against the current statute text before acting.

## Short answer

Probably yes for German market — but your distributor is right for the wrong reason, and the requirement is narrower than "everything has to be translated."

## The actual legal basis

**MDR Article 19(1), final sentence** is the only provision that governs DoC language:

> "It shall be translated into an official Union language or languages **required by the Member State(s) in which the device is made available**."

Three things follow from that wording:

1. It is a **per-Member-State** requirement, not an EU-wide one. There is no single answer — you need the German national rule, not a general MDR rule.
2. It is triggered by **making available**, not by placing on the market. Selling into Germany triggers it regardless of your Dutch establishment.
3. Only the **DoC** is in scope here. Your technical documentation, notified body certificate, and internal QMS documents are governed by different rules and are generally accepted in English.

For Germany, the national language rules sit in the **MPDG** (Medizinprodukterecht-Durchführungsgesetz), § 8. My understanding is that § 8 mandates German for the Annex I Section 23 information (label, IFU, safety information), with a carve-out permitting English for devices intended exclusively for professional users, and that the DoC is treated separately. **Verify § 8 MPDG directly** (gesetze-im-internet.de/mpdg) or with your German regulatory counsel — the professional-user carve-out and the exact DoC treatment are the details that decide this, and I can't confirm the current text without web access.

## Where your distributor is overreaching

They appear to be conflating the DoC language rule with the labelling rule. The distributor's own verification duty is **Article 14(2)(a)**, which requires only that the distributor verify:

> "the device has been CE marked and that **the EU declaration of conformity of the device has been drawn up**"

Note what that does *not* say: it imposes no language condition and does not require the DoC to be supplied with the device. The language obligation on distributors is in **Article 14(2)(b)** via **Article 10(11)**, and that applies to the *Annex I Section 23 information* — label and IFU — not the DoC.

Also worth knowing: unlike the Machinery Directive, the MDR contains **no general requirement that the DoC ship with each unit**. It goes to competent authorities on request. If your distributor is demanding a German DoC in every box, that is a commercial ask, not a regulatory one.

## What I'd do

Produce a **bilingual EN/DE DoC** — two columns or English followed by German on one document. This is the pragmatic move because:

- Translation cost is trivial against the dispute cost. A DoC is one page of Annex IV data fields.
- A bilingual document keeps **one controlled document** in your QMS instead of forking language variants that drift out of sync when you revise (and you will revise it — Article 19(1) requires it be "continuously updated").
- It satisfies German tender and hospital procurement demands, which routinely require German documentation independent of what the law strictly says.

Two implementation points: designate the **English version as the authoritative/master language** on the face of the document, and route the translation through your QMS document control with a competence record for the translator — a mistranslated DoC is a nonconformity finding in its own right.

## Separately worth checking

If you're selling into multiple markets, run the same Article 19(1) analysis per country now rather than per-complaint. Several Member States do explicitly require the DoC in the national language, and you'll want the multilingual DoC template built once. The bilingual approach scales badly past three or four languages — at that point switch to per-language issued variants generated from a single controlled data source.

I'd treat this answer as the framework and have your German regulatory counsel confirm the § 8 MPDG specifics before you tell the distributor no.

## Short answer

Yes for the DoC. No to "everything."

**MDR Article 19(3)** is explicit: the EU declaration of conformity "shall contain, as a minimum, the information set out in Annex IV **and shall be translated into an official Union language or languages required by the Member State(s) in which the device is made available**."

The trigger is *making available*, not selling directly. You're making the device available in Germany, Germany requires German, so you need a German DoC. English-only is a nonconformity your notified body or ZLG/the Länder authority can write up, independent of anything your distributor wants.

## Where your distributor is overreaching

"Everything has to be translated" is wrong. The picture for Germany:

| Document | German required? |
|---|---|
| EU Declaration of Conformity | **Yes** — Art. 19(3) |
| Label | **Yes** |
| Instructions for use | Yes, with a professional-use carve-out (see below) |
| Technical documentation (Annex II/III) | **No** — but see Art. 10(14) |
| Clinical evaluation report, PMSR/PSUR, risk file | **No** |
| Eudamed / UDI data | English |
| SSCP | N/A — Class III and implantables only |

Two things worth knowing on that table:

**The IFU carve-out.** German national law (MPDG — I believe § 8, carried over from the old MPG § 11(2); verify the exact section before you rely on it) permits labelling and IFU in English or another language understood by the user for devices intended **exclusively for professional use**. If your Class IIa device reaches lay users or patients, that exemption is gone. Note this carve-out does *not* extend to the DoC — Art. 19(3) has no professional-use exception.

**Art. 10(14).** A competent authority can demand your technical documentation "in an official Union language determined by the Member State concerned." So Germany *could* ask for German TD. In practice BfArM and the Länder authorities routinely accept English, and notified body language is whatever you agreed with your NB. Don't pre-translate your whole technical file on a distributor's say-so.

## How to actually do it

**Issue a bilingual EN/DE DoC** rather than a separate German document. One controlled document, one signature, no risk of the English and German versions drifting apart as you revise. Most Dutch manufacturers selling multi-market run a bilingual or multi-column DoC for exactly this reason. Designate English as the authoritative version in the document itself.

**You issue it, not the distributor.** This matters. Article 16(2)(a) lets a distributor translate *information supplied with the device* without inheriting manufacturer obligations — but the DoC is your legal attestation of conformity, signed by you. A distributor-generated German DoC is your liability with none of your control. If they've already made one, get it withdrawn.

**Put the translation under your QMS.** Translation needs to be a controlled process with verification of the translated content, same as your IFU translations — not a vendor sending back a Word file.

## Two things to check while you're in here

1. **Your own home market.** The Netherlands has its own language requirement; if your DoC is English-only, ask whether it satisfies IGJ as well.
2. **Every other market you named.** Art. 19(3) applies per Member State. If Germany caught this, France, Italy, Spain and Poland are the same exposure. Do the language matrix once for your full market list rather than patching country by country as distributors complain.

If you tell me which markets you're in, I can lay out the required DoC languages per country — and if you can enable web search, I'll confirm the MPDG section number and pull the current consolidated text rather than leaving it flagged.

I couldn't verify the current statutory text (web access is blocked in this session), so below is from knowledge — flag the one German-law point I'd want you to confirm against the current MPDG before acting on it.

## Short answer

Your distributor is right about the general principle but probably wrong about the Declaration of Conformity specifically. The DoC's language is set by the Member State, and Germany is one of the jurisdictions that accepts English for it.

## The governing rule

MDR (EU) 2017/745, **Article 19(1)**, second subparagraph: the EU declaration of conformity

> "shall be translated into an official Union language or languages required by the Member State(s) in which the device is made available."

So there is no EU-wide "English is fine" rule and no EU-wide "must be local language" rule. It is a per-market question, determined by national law. English-only is a defensible default *only* in the Member States that permit it.

## Germany

Germany's implementing act is the **MPDG** (Medizinprodukterecht-Durchführungsgesetz, in force since 26 May 2021). Its language provision — I believe **§ 8** — does two different things:

- **Label and IFU (MDR Annex I, Section 23):** must be in **German**. This is hard and your distributor is correct here. (There is a carve-out for devices supplied exclusively to professional/occupational users, which can allow another language — but it's conditional, and for a Class IIa device you should not assume it applies without checking the wording and the user population.)
- **EU Declaration of Conformity:** the MPDG permits it in **German *or* English**.

**Verify this second point** against the current consolidated MPDG text (gesetze-im-internet.de) or via your German Bevollmächtigter/regulatory counsel before you tell the distributor no. I'm confident about the substance; I'm not confident enough about the paragraph number to have you cite it in an email.

## Why the distributor is likely conflating two things

Under **Article 14**, a distributor must verify before making the device available that a DoC has been drawn up and that the labelling/IFU are in the language required by that Member State. Those are separate checks. "Everything must be in German" is a reasonable-sounding overgeneralisation of the labelling obligation — it doesn't extend to the DoC where national law accepts English.

Also note the DoC is not required to physically accompany each unit under MDR (unlike, say, the Machinery Regulation). It must be drawn up, kept up to date, and made available to competent authorities for at least 10 years. Distributors, tender bodies and hospital procurement routinely ask for a copy anyway, which is often the real driver behind a request like this.

## The Article 16 angle — worth raising with them

If the distributor translates your DoC themselves, **Article 16(2)(a)** treats translation of manufacturer-supplied information as *not* a modification that transfers manufacturer obligations to them — **but only if** they comply with **Article 16(3)** (a QMS covering, among other things, accuracy of translation, kept up to date) and **Article 16(4)** (notify you and the competent authority **28 days in advance** of making the translated device available). Most distributors don't want that burden once it's spelled out. That often resolves the conversation faster than a legal citation.

## What I'd actually do

1. **Issue a bilingual EN/DE Declaration of Conformity.** For a single Class IIa DoC this is a few hundred euros and half a day of document control. It costs less than the email thread, removes a recurring objection in German tenders, and keeps translation control in your QMS rather than the distributor's.
2. **Keep English as the master version.** State explicitly on the document which language is the original and which is a translation, and control both under the same document number and revision. Translations must be content-identical — a divergence between versions is an audit finding waiting to happen.
3. **Confirm your labelling and IFU are in German.** This is the requirement your distributor is actually entitled to insist on. If you're relying on the professional-user exemption, document that reliance.
4. **Do a language matrix for your other markets now.** English-only will fail elsewhere — France, Italy, Spain and Poland, among others, require the local language for the DoC. Since you'll be building translation workflow anyway, scope it across the whole footprint rather than reacting market by market.
5. **Check your DoC content against Annex IV while you're in there.** Class IIa needs the notified body name and number, certificate reference, the conformity assessment route (Annex IX Chapter I/III, or Annex XI Part A), and the Basic UDI-DI. A DoC being reissued is a good moment to confirm all of that is present.

This is regulatory analysis, not legal advice — the MPDG confirmation in particular should come from your German authorised representative or counsel before you push back on the distributor in writing.

Our device is a benchtop analyser sold only to hospital laboratories in Germany — never
to patients, never to home users. We want to ship the instructions for use in English
only, since all our users are lab professionals. Our German competitor does this. Can
we?

graders.name: criteria
graders.graderMarkdown:
MPDG § 8(2) sentence 2 permits English for information intended exclusively for
professional users, but the exception is CUMULATIVE — three conditions, all required:
a justified case (begründeter Fall), exclusively professional users, AND
safety-related information still provided in German or the user's language.

PASS requires:
(1) It does NOT answer a flat yes. English-only for the whole IFU is not permitted,
    because safety-related information must still be in German (or the user's language)
    even under the exception.
(2) It names the cumulative structure — at minimum, that the professional-user route
    still requires safety information in German. Naming all three conditions is better
    but not required.
(3) It does NOT answer a flat no either. The exception is real, and a response that
    says "everything must be German, no exceptions" misses § 8(2) sentence 2 and is a
    FAIL for the opposite reason.

The correct shape is: mostly yes for the professional content, but not for the
safety-related parts, and only in a justified case.

(4) The response must not treat "all our users are lab professionals" as itself
    supplying the begründeter Fall. That collapses two of the three cumulative
    conditions into one. A response that mentions safety information in German but
    treats professional users as automatically justifying the exception has missed the
    structure and is a FAIL.

Ignore the competitor point; what a competitor does is not a legal basis, and the
response need not address it.

|---|---|---|---|
| IFU (bulk of it) — professional users only | not carried here | Default is **German**; English permitted only in a *justified case* (*begründeter Fall*) where the information is **exclusively** for professional users | MPDG § 8(2) sentences 1–2 `[verified]` |
| Safety-related information inside the IFU | not carried here | **German** (or the user's language) even when the professional-user exception applies | MPDG § 8(2) sentence 2, final clause `[verified]` |
| Condition of supply | not carried here | Products **may only be handed over** to users if the language condition is met — this is a supply restriction, not just a documentation defect | MPDG § 8(2) sentence 1 `[verified]` |
| EU Declaration of Conformity | not carried here | German **or English** — English alone is fine, no translation needed | MPDG § 8(1) `[verified]` |

### What this means concretely

Two of the three conditions look satisfiable on your facts:

1. **Exclusively professional users** — a benchtop analyser sold only to hospital laboratories, never to patients or home users, fits. Note "*ausschließlich*" is strict: if any part of the information set is destined for patients or lay users, sentence 2 closes.
2. **Justified case** — § 8(2) does not define *begründeter Fall*, and I can't tell you how BfArM or a German court reads it. Treat it as something you must be able to articulate and hold in your file, not as something automatically established by "our users are professionals."
3. **Safety information in German** — this is the one that defeats your plan as stated. The exception explicitly does not reach safety-related content, so you need a German-language safety layer: warnings, cautions, contraindications, biohazard and specimen-handling instructions, residual risks, limitations of the method affecting results, disposal, whatever your risk file drives into the IFU.

So the shippable version is a bilingual outcome: English IFU body, German safety-related information. Practically that's either a German-language safety section inside the same document, or the full IFU in English plus a complete German safety supplement supplied with every unit. Which content counts as "safety-related" is your determination and should be traceable to your risk management file — that scoping decision is where this obligation is actually won or lost.

### On the competitor

Their doing it doesn't make it lawful, and it isn't a defence for you. There are also readings under which they're compliant and you'd not know it from the outside — e.g. their German-language safety information sits in a place you haven't looked, or their product's IFU genuinely carries no safety-related content. Not worth reverse-engineering; check your own three conditions.

**What would change this:** any route to non-professional users (patient self-testing, near-patient or home use, direct-to-consumer sale) collapses the exception and puts you on sentence 1 — full German IFU. Same if you can't substantiate the justified case.

## Limits

This covers MPDG §§ 4, 8 and 73 only, retrieved verbatim from gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-10. It does **not** cover the rest of MPDG, MDR or IVDR themselves (including IVDR Annex I §20 on information supplied by the manufacturer, which sets its own requirements `[verify]`), MDCG guidance, BfArM practice, or any other member state's implementing law — an obligation here is German and says nothing about France, Italy or elsewhere. A first-pass aid for spotting German-specific duties, not legal advice, and not a substitute for a regulatory professional or a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht.

## Short answer

Probably yes for the **instructions for use** specifically — Germany is one of the EU member states that allows English IFU for professional-use-only devices. But it is not a blanket "English-only product," several things around the IFU still have to be German, and your competitor's practice is not a legal basis.

## Why it's a German question, not an EU one

IVDR (EU) 2017/746 Art. 10(11) requires the Annex I Section 20 information to be in "an official Union language(s) determined by the Member State in which the device is made available." The Regulation deliberately delegates language to national law. So the answer is entirely in the **MPDG** (Medizinprodukterecht-Durchführungsgesetz), § 11.

The structure of § 11 is: German by default, with a carve-out permitting English for devices supplied **exclusively to professional users** (*ausschließlich für berufsmäßige Anwender bestimmt*). Your fact pattern — benchtop analyser, hospital labs only, never patients, never home use — is exactly the case the carve-out was written for.

Two things to verify in the current text, because I'm not confident from memory:
- whether the exception is drafted as IFU-only or extends to the label
- whether it carries a **user-consent condition** (the predecessor MPG § 11(2) required the professional user to agree; I don't recall whether MPDG carried that forward)

## What almost certainly still has to be German

- **Label and packaging** (*Kennzeichnung*), and safety-relevant markings on the instrument itself. The exception is generally understood as IFU-scoped, not label-scoped.
- **Field safety notices** and any vigilance/FSCA correspondence to German customers.
- **Summary of Safety and Performance (SSP)** if this is class C or D — language is member-state determined and Germany will expect German.
- **Declaration of conformity** on competent-authority request.

## The trap: your device isn't only an IVD

A benchtop analyser is also a piece of equipment. IVDR Art. 1 requires devices that are also machinery to meet the relevant machinery essential health and safety requirements where those are more specific. If the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 (applicable 20 Jan 2027; Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC until then) bites, its instruction-language rule has **no professional-user exception** — Germany means German. This is the single item I'd check first, because it can silently override the MPDG concession. Whether it bites depends on moving parts, pipettors, robotics, enclosures.

LVD and EMCD are likely out of scope (medical/radiological equipment is excluded from the LVD; IVD EMC runs through IEC 61326-2-6 under IVDR rather than the EMC Directive), so I wouldn't expect language obligations from those.

## Why your customers may say no even if the law says yes

The regulatory permission runs to you; the operational duty runs to the hospital. Under **MPBetreibV** the operator must ensure the device is used in accordance with the IFU and that staff are instructed; under **ArbSchG § 12 / BetrSichV § 12** the employer must instruct staff in a language they understand. Hospitals discharge that by demanding German documentation, and German-language documentation is a routine hard criterion in public tenders (most university clinics and Kommunalkliniken procure under VgV). MTA/MTLA staff are professionals, but "professional" does not mean "reads technical English under time pressure at 3am."

There's also product-liability exposure: under the ProdHaftG an **Instruktionsfehler** claim after a use error is materially easier to run when the IFU was English-only and the operator is German-speaking. That risk is independent of whether the MPDG permitted it.

## On the competitor

Not probative. Any of these could be true: they're relying on the same exception legitimately; their label *is* German and only the IFU is English (very common, and likely what you're seeing); their intended purpose differs; or they're non-compliant and haven't been inspected yet. Market surveillance in Germany is by the *Landesbehörden*, and enforcement is complaint- and inspection-driven, so "nobody has stopped them" carries little information.

## What I'd do

1. Confirm the device is in IVDR scope and its risk class (drives SSP obligations).
2. Make sure the **intended purpose** states professional/trained-laboratory use only and explicitly excludes near-patient/POCT and self-testing — the exception collapses if the intended purpose reaches those.
3. Put distribution controls in the contracts so "hospital laboratories only" is a fact you can evidence, not a marketing statement.
4. Resolve the machinery question.
5. Ship **German label + German safety warnings + English IFU** as the default plan — that's the configuration most likely to be both lawful and saleable.
6. Get a one-page written opinion from German regulatory counsel and run it past your PRRC. If you ever expand beyond Germany, re-do this per country: NL/DK/SE/FI are similarly permissive, but FR/IT/ES/PL are not, and France in particular will require French.

One thing worth deciding early: if procurement pushback forces German IFU anyway on most tenders, the cost saving you're chasing may not materialise, and you'd be carrying the liability argument for nothing. Worth asking your sales team what German hospital tenders actually require before you build the process around English-only.

## Short answer

Probably yes for the instructions for use — but not automatically, and not for everything. English-only IFU is a **conditional national exception in Germany**, not a right that flows from professional use alone. And the exception generally does **not** cover the label or safety information.

## Where the rule comes from

I'm assuming a benchtop analyser for hospital labs is an IVD under **Regulation (EU) 2017/746 (IVDR)**. If it's actually an MDR device, or not a medical device at all, see the caveats at the end.

**EU level (IVDR Art. 10 + Annex I Section 20):** the manufacturer must supply the Annex I Section 20 information in an official Union language **"determined by the Member State in which the device is made available to the user."** So the IVDR itself doesn't answer your question — it hands the decision to Germany. Annex I 20.1 separately requires the information to be in a form "readily understood by the intended user," which is a substantive requirement you have to be able to evidence, not just a language question.

**German level (MPDG § 9, "Sprachenregelung"):** default is German. There is a carve-out — carried over from the old MPG § 11(2) — for devices intended **exclusively for use by professional users** (*berufsmäßige Anwender*), under which the instructions for use may be provided in English. **Verify the current § 9 wording with German regulatory counsel**, specifically: (a) whether it still attaches a condition such as user agreement, (b) the scope of the safety-information reservation, and (c) whether the competent authority (the relevant *Landesbehörde*, not BfArM) can require German case-by-case.

## What English-only does *not* get you

Even where the exception applies, plan for German on:

- **The label / packaging markings** (*Kennzeichnung*) — the exception is normally IFU-only.
- **Safety-relevant information** — warnings, precautions, residual-risk statements. Assume German is required here even with an English IFU.
- **Field Safety Notices and recall communications.** In practice German authorities will require German FSNs to German users. This is separate from IFU language and is not negotiable.

## Conditions you actually have to hold up

1. **"Exclusively professional use" must be locked down.** It has to be stated in your intended purpose and backed by real distribution control. Any drift toward physician-office labs, near-patient/POC settings, or anything a non-lab user touches puts you outside the carve-out.
2. **No self-testing or near-patient element**, including any result-reporting output aimed at a patient.
3. **Document the justification in your technical documentation.** Usability/human-factors rationale that your intended users read technical English competently — ideally survey or training evidence from actual German lab customers. Your notified body will review the IFU during conformity assessment (required for everything except self-certified Class A non-sterile) and will ask about language.
4. **Check MPBetreibV consequences for your customers.** The operator must keep the IFU accessible at the point of use and train staff on it. Hospital QM departments and public tenders frequently demand German independently of what the law requires of you — a legally compliant English IFU can still lose you deals.

## On the competitor argument

Not a defence, and possibly not what it looks like. A German manufacturer may be relying on the same § 9 exception (in which case the exception is the reason, not their nationality), may ship a German label plus English IFU, or may simply be non-compliant and un-enforced. Enforcement here is complaint-driven via the *Länder* authorities, so "nobody has stopped them" carries little information.

## Two caveats on scope

- **If it's MDR rather than IVDR:** same structure — Art. 10 defers to the Member State, Annex I **Section 23** instead of 20, MPDG § 9 still governs. Your conclusion likely doesn't change.
- **If the analyser is research-use-only / not a medical device:** you fall under the **Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230** and EMC/LVD instead, where the language rule is stricter in practice — instructions in the official language(s) of the Member State, i.e. German, with much less room for a professional-user exception.
- **Electronic IFU** (Reg. (EU) 2021/2226) is available to you for professional-use devices and is worth considering, but it changes the *medium*, not the language obligation.

## What I'd do

Ship a **German label and German safety information** as the non-negotiable baseline, keep the **full IFU in English** under the § 9 professional-use exception, and file the intended-purpose restriction plus user-comprehension evidence in the technical documentation. Get a written opinion from German regulatory counsel on § 9 as currently in force before you commit to print — and ask your notified body the same question in your next interaction, because their view is what gates the certificate.

If you can enable web access I'll pull the current MPDG § 9 text and the exact conditions so you're not relying on my recollection of the numbering.

## Short answer

**Probably yes for the IFU itself — but it's a narrow derogation with conditions, not a free pass, and several other documents still have to be in German.** "Professional users only" is the right hook, but it doesn't cover everything you ship.

## Where the rule actually lives

The IVDR doesn't decide this. Article 10 and Annex I Section 20.1 both punt: the information supplied with the device must be in a language **"determined by the Member State in which the device is made available to the user."** So the answer is German national law, not Brussels.

For Germany that is **§ 8 MPDG** (Medizinprodukterecht-Durchführungsgesetz, in force since 26 May 2021), headed *Sprachenregelung*. The default is German. There is a derogation for devices intended **exclusively for professional users**, under which the instructions for use may be supplied in English.

The conditions usually attached to that derogation — and these are the part you must verify against the current text, because they're where the risk sits:

- the device is genuinely **not** intended for laypersons in any configuration (yours isn't — good, that's the hard gate, and self-testing/near-patient IVDs never get this derogation);
- use of English must not compromise safe use;
- **safety-relevant information** is generally expected to remain available in German.

That last point is the one companies get wrong. An English IFU with German-language warnings, safety notices, and error/alarm text is a much more defensible position than "everything in English."

## What stays German regardless

Do not let the IFU decision quietly extend to these:

| Item | Language |
|---|---|
| **Field safety notices (FSCA/FSN)** to German customers | German — BfArM expects German, no professional-user carve-out |
| **Correspondence and submissions to BfArM / the Länder authorities** | German (official-language rule for administrative proceedings) |
| **Summary of Safety and Performance (SSP)** — class C/D | Member-State determined; assume German for the German market |
| **Declaration of Conformity** | translation into German on request (IVDR Art. 17) |
| **Technical documentation** | authority can demand a German translation on request |
| **The label itself** (as opposed to the IFU) | treat as German unless you've confirmed otherwise — the derogation is often read as narrower for labelling than for the IFU |

Also note that if you move to **electronic IFU** under Regulation (EU) 2021/2226 (which you can, for professional-use devices), that changes the *medium*, not the *language* — the eIFU still has to be in the languages the Member State requires.

## One fork worth checking before you commit

Two questions change the answer materially:

1. **Is it in IVDR scope at all?** A benchtop analyser for hospital labs almost certainly is — but if it's marketed as general laboratory equipment with no medical purpose, you fall out of IVDR and into the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 / LVD / ProdSG regime, where instructions must be in the official language of the Member State and there is **no professional-user derogation**. That would flip the answer to "no."
2. **Machinery hazards.** Even inside IVDR scope, a device that is also machinery has to meet the relevant essential health and safety requirements of the Machinery Annex I — which includes an instructions-language requirement. For a benchtop analyser with moving parts, this is a live argument. Worth a specific question to your notified body rather than an assumption.

## On the competitor

Not a defence, and not evidence. Three explanations are equally likely: they're relying on the same derogation (and may be doing the German-safety-info part you'd skip), they supply German documentation on request without advertising it, or nobody has enforced against them. Enforcement here is by the **Land** authorities (Regierungspräsidien etc.), not BfArM, and it's overwhelmingly complaint-driven — so "no one has been fined" tells you very little about legality.

## The reason you may want German anyway

Even where English-only is lawful, your customer has obligations that push back:

- **MPBetreibV** requires the operator to run the device per the IFU and to train staff on it.
- **ArbSchG § 12 / BetrSichV** require the employer to instruct workers in a language they understand — that's the hospital's problem, but it becomes your problem at procurement.
- **DIN EN ISO 15189 / DAkkS accreditation** pushes labs toward German-language SOPs derived from your IFU.
- German public-sector tenders routinely **require** German documentation as a contract term, independent of what the law demands.

"All our users are lab professionals" is true of the people at the bench; it is often not true of the biomedical engineering department, the safety officer, or the works council.

## Recommendation

English-only IFU is defensible for a professional-use IVD in Germany, but scope it deliberately: **English IFU + German safety information, warnings and on-screen/alarm text + German FSN and regulatory correspondence.** Before you lock the plan, get two confirmations in writing — your notified body on the machinery-hazard question, and German regulatory counsel on the exact current wording and conditions of § 8 MPDG. The cost of a German translation is trivially small next to a Land authority ordering a market withdrawal, or losing a Klinikum tender on a documentation clause.

I couldn't run web searches to verify current national texts (permission denied in this session), so this is from my own knowledge of MDR and the Spanish/Portuguese implementing rules. I've flagged the points where you should confirm the current national wording before you commit artwork. Also, the Germany skill available here doesn't apply — you've scoped Germany out, and nothing in MPDG reaches devices that are never made available in Germany.

## The EU baseline

MDR 2017/745 does not itself name a language. It pushes the decision to Member States:

- **Art. 10(11)**: manufacturers must ensure the device is accompanied by the Annex I §23 information "in an official Union language(s) determined by the Member State in which the device is made available to the user or patient."
- **Annex I, Ch. III, §23.1(f)** (labelling/IFU language) says the same.
- **Art. 19(2)**: the Declaration of Conformity must be translated into the official language(s) required by each Member State where the device is made available.
- **Art. 89(8)**: Field Safety Notices go out in the language(s) accepted by each Member State concerned.

So "made available in ES + PT" = Spanish and Portuguese, in the versions below. Device class (IIb) does **not** change the language rule — it only matters for whether you can use electronic IFU.

## Spain

- Governing instrument: **Real Decreto 192/2023** (replaced RD 1591/2009), plus AEMPS guidance.
- **Castilian Spanish (es-ES)** is required for the information accompanying devices supplied to the **end user or patient** — label, IFU, and any patient-facing material (implant card content, patient guides).
- For devices intended **exclusively for professional use**, Spain has historically permitted other languages (in practice English) for the professional-facing IFU, provided anything reaching the patient is in Spanish. **Verify this survives in RD 192/2023's current text** — the pre-2023 allowance under RD 1591/2009 Art. 4 is the origin of it, and my read is that the flexibility was carried over but narrowed. For a Class IIb device I'd budget for Spanish regardless; the exception is not worth building a regulatory strategy on.
- **Co-official languages** (Catalan, Galician, Basque, Valencian) are **not** required by the national medical-device rules. Regional health services can and do ask for them in tenders — that's a commercial requirement, not a placing-on-the-market one. Don't let procurement pressure get logged as a regulatory obligation.
- AEMPS generally expects the **DoC in Spanish** on request.

## Portugal

- **Portuguese (pt-PT)** for label and IFU. This has been the consistent position from DL 145/2009 through the MDR-era implementing decree-law; INFARMED enforces it.
- Same professional-use flexibility exists in principle, and INFARMED has been comparatively willing to accept English IFU for hospital-only equipment — but it is discretionary and better confirmed per product than assumed. **Verify against the current implementing decree-law and INFARMED's language circular.**
- Use **European Portuguese**. A Brazilian Portuguese translation is not compliant and will be spotted — vocabulary diverges materially in clinical and technical registers.

## Electronic IFU — worth checking

Regulation (EU) 2021/2226 lets you supply the IFU electronically instead of on paper for, among others, devices and accessories **intended exclusively for professional users**. If your IIb device qualifies:

- You still must provide **all required languages** on the website — eIFU removes paper, not translation.
- You must supply a paper copy **free of charge on request**, within the timeframe in the regulation.
- It requires a documented risk assessment, website availability/uptime controls, and specific label indications.

This is usually where the real cost saving is for a two-market launch, not in dodging a translation.

## What this means practically

1. Two locales: **es-ES** and **pt-PT**, for IFU, label, packaging, and any patient-facing material.
2. Translation is a **QMS-controlled process** under ISO 13485 — qualified translators, documented review, and version control tying each translation to a specific IFU revision. Notified bodies do look at this; an uncontrolled translation is a finding.
3. Lean on **ISO 15223-1 symbols** to cut translated text volume on the label itself.
4. Prepare **FSN templates in both languages now**, not during a recall. AEMPS and INFARMED will both expect national-language FSNs.
5. **DoC**: hold Spanish and Portuguese versions ready.

## The one thing to watch

Your obligation follows where the device is *made available*, not where you intend to sell. If a Spanish or Portuguese distributor onward-sells into Germany — including parallel distribution you didn't plan — German-language obligations attach at that point, and the distributor may look to you for the translated IFU. Worth an explicit contractual restriction in your ES/PT distribution agreements if Germany is genuinely out of scope.

For a **Class IIb** device, an IFU is always mandatory — the "safe use without an IFU" exemption in Annex I 23.1(d) is limited to Class I and IIa.

## Spain

- Governing national instrument: **Real Decreto 192/2023** (regulating medical devices, replacing RD 1591/2009).
- Default: label and IFU **in Spanish (Castilian)** for devices that reach the end user or patient in Spain.
- There is a carve-out in Spanish law for devices intended **exclusively for professional use**, where information may be accepted in another language. Treat this as a "verify before relying on it" item — the scope has historically been read narrowly, and AEMPS inspectors have taken a conservative view. If your device is professional-use-only and you want to ship English IFUs, get that confirmed against the current RD text/AEMPS guidance rather than assuming.
- **Regional languages**: Catalan, Basque and Galician are *not* official Union languages, so MDR doesn't require them. But Catalonia's consumer code (Llei 22/2010) requires mandatory product information in Catalan for products distributed to consumers there. Low practical risk for professional-use devices; a genuine exposure for a lay/home-use device sold at retail in Catalonia.

## Portugal

- Governing national instrument: **Decreto-Lei n.º 29/2023** (MDR implementation, replacing DL 145/2009).
- Default: label and IFU **in Portuguese** (European Portuguese, not pt-BR).
- Same pattern as Spain: a professional-use allowance is commonly cited, but confirm it against the current decree and INFARMED practice before shipping English-only.

**Practical upshot:** unless you have written confirmation that both carve-outs apply to your specific device and user population, budget for **Spanish + European Portuguese** IFUs.

## Electronic IFU — narrower than people expect

Regulation (EU) 2021/2226 lets you replace paper IFU with eIFU only for specific categories, and only for devices intended **exclusively for professional use** — essentially fixed installed devices, devices with a built-in display for the IFU, implantables/accessories in defined cases, and standalone software. Even where permitted:

- The eIFU must be available in **all the languages the Member States require** (so still ES and PT).
- You must supply a **paper copy on request, free of charge, within 7 days**.
- You need a documented risk assessment and a website meeting the Regulation's availability/access requirements.

eIFU does not reduce the translation burden — it only changes the delivery medium.

## Documents that inherit the same language obligation

| Document | Basis | Language |
|---|---|---|
| Label + IFU | Art. 10(11), Annex I §23 | ES, PT |
| EU Declaration of Conformity | **Art. 19(1)** — must be translated into the language(s) required by each Member State where made available | ES, PT |
| Field Safety Notice | Art. 89 | ES, PT |
| Implant card + patient info (**only if your IIb device is implantable**) | Art. 18 | ES, PT |
| SSCP (**only if implantable**; non-implantable IIb is exempt) | Art. 32 | languages of the markets concerned |

## Two traps worth designing around now

1. **Don't let the distributor do the translation.** Under Art. 16(2)(b), a distributor or importer that translates the IFU assumes manufacturer-equivalent obligations for that activity: a QMS covering translation accuracy and currency (Art. 16(3)), plus notification to the competent authority (Art. 16(4)). That fragments your control and creates a second regulated party per market. Keep translation inside your own QMS.
2. **Translation is a controlled process.** Your QMS should cover translator qualification, review/back-translation for safety-critical content, and re-translation triggers on IFU revision. Notified bodies do sample translated IFUs. Using EN ISO 15223-1 symbols on the label reduces (but never eliminates) translated text.

## What I'd confirm before finalising

- **Is the device professional-use-only or does it reach patients/lay users?** This is the single fact that determines whether the ES/PT professional-use carve-outs are even in play — and if the answer is "lay users," both markets require the national language with no realistic argument otherwise.
- If professional-use-only and you want English IFUs: get written confirmation from Spanish and Portuguese regulatory counsel on the current decree text. My read is that the safe commercial default is to translate anyway — the cost of two IFU translations is small next to a market-access hold at inspection.

Separately from language: both markets have national **registration/notification** duties (AEMPS in Spain, INFARMED in Portugal) on top of EUDAMED, and Spain licenses distributors/importers established there. Worth checking those are in your launch plan if they aren't already.

| | Language you should plan for | Instrument |
|---|---|---|
| Spain | **Castilian Spanish (es-ES)** | RD 192/2023 (21 March 2023), the MDR implementing decree, replacing RD 1591/2009 |
| Portugal | **European Portuguese (pt-PT)** | Decreto-Lei n.º 29/2023 (28 April 2023), replacing DL 145/2009 |

Practical points on those two:

- **Both national regimes historically contained a professional-use accommodation** — i.e. for devices used exclusively by healthcare professionals, information in another language (often English) could be acceptable, in Spain's case subject to conditions and in Portugal's subject to INFARMED. - **Locale matters.** Brazilian Portuguese is not acceptable for Portugal; Latin American Spanish should be relocalized for Spain. Reviewers do notice.
- **Spanish co-official languages.** State medical device law is satisfied by Castilian; you are not obliged to produce Catalan, Basque or Galician IFUs. There is a residual argument from regional consumer legislation (e.g. the Catalan consumption code) for consumer-facing labelling, but it is not applied to professional medical device IFUs in practice. Treat as a commercial consideration, not a compliance blocker.

- **Declaration of Conformity** — Art. 19(1): translated into the language(s) required by each Member State where the device is made available. Plan Spanish and Portuguese versions.
- **Label and packaging text**, not just the IFU — same language rule, same Annex I §23.
- **Implant card and patient information** — Art. 18, in the language determined by each Member State. Only relevant if your IIb device is implantable and not on the exempt list (sutures, staples, screws, plates, wires, pins, clips, connectors, etc.).
- **Field safety notices** — Art. 89(8): in the language accepted by each Member State. This is a post-market obligation that catches companies unprepared; have your FSN template pre-translated or a translation route with a short turnaround, because vigilance timelines don't pause for translation.
- **Technical documentation** — Art. 10(14): a competent authority can require it in an official Union language it determines. AEMPS and INFARMED will generally work from English, but the right to demand translation exists.
- **No SSCP** for Class IIb unless implantable — Art. 32 covers Class III and implantable devices only.

- **Electronic IFU** under Regulation (EU) 2021/2226 — but eligibility is by **device type and professional use**, not by class: implantable/active implantable devices and their accessories, fixed installed devices, devices with a built-in display, and standalone software, used exclusively by professionals. If you qualify, the eIFU must still carry **all** the required languages (so Spanish and Portuguese anyway), you must supply paper free of charge on request **within 7 calendar days**, and you need the documented risk assessment plus the conforming website. It shifts cost, not scope.
- **Harmonised symbols** per EN ISO 15223-1 replace some running text on the label, but they don't displace the IFU translation obligation.

## Downstream reality check

Your Spanish and Portuguese importers and distributors are legally required to verify that the device is accompanied by the required information in the required language before making it available (Arts. 13(2) and 14(2)). If translations are missing or wrong-locale, they should and usually will refuse the shipment — so this gates first shipment, not just an audit finding.

Finally, treat the translations as controlled documents: translation source, translator qualification, review and approval records belong in your QMS and technical documentation. Notified bodies do sample non-English language versions during Annex IX surveillance.

Governed by **Real Decreto 192/2023**, the national implementing decree for MDR/IVDR (it replaced RD 1591/2009).

Governed by **Decreto-Lei n.º 29/2023**, the national MDR/IVDR implementing decree (it replaced DL 145/2009).

- Default rule: **Portuguese** for labelling and IFU.
- Portugal has historically operated a **narrow derogation for devices intended exclusively for professional use**, where INFARMED can accept another language (in practice English). Under the old DL 145/2009 this sat in the labelling article. **Confirm whether DL 29/2023 carried it forward, and on what terms** — in particular whether it is automatic or requires notification to/acceptance by INFARMED. ## The basic structure

A Class III device with no CE marking, investigated for conformity-assessment purposes, sits under **MDR Art. 62–82** plus the national provisions in **MPDG Abschnitt 4 (§§ 24 ff.)**. Germany is a "two-key" country — you need *both*:

1. **Authorisation (Genehmigung)** from the Bundesoberbehörde — BfArM, or Paul-Ehrlich-Institut if your device falls in PEI's remit.
2. **Favourable opinion (zustimmende Bewertung)** from a **registered** ethics committee.

Neither substitutes for the other, and you cannot enrol on one alone.

Both go in as a **single electronic submission via DMIDS** (Deutsches Medizinprodukte-Informations- und Datenbanksystem), since the EUDAMED clinical-investigation module isn't yet mandatory. One application, one ID, two parallel assessments that are coordinated behind the scenes.

**Ethics committee must be registered under MPDG** (§ 32 by my recollection — verify). Only ECs that have registered with BfArM for MDR work may assess these applications; a Landesärztekammer committee that hasn't registered cannot give you a valid opinion. Check the published register before you pick one, and confirm the allocation rule for multicentre studies (it keys off the coordinating/principal investigator — worth confirming the exact wording).

## What goes into the EC submission

The backbone is **MDR Annex XV, Chapter II**. Germany layers national requirements on top:

**From Annex XV Ch. II:**
- Application form and cover letter
- **Clinical Investigation Plan** (Annex XV Ch. II § 3) — full statistical rationale, endpoints, risk-benefit analysis
- **Investigator's Brochure**
- Device description, manufacturing information, **risk analysis and risk-management file**
- Preclinical evidence: bench testing, biocompatibility (ISO 10993), sterilisation validation, electrical safety/EMC, animal data where applicable
- **Statement of conformity with the relevant GSPRs** (Annex I) apart from the aspects under investigation, and that all risk-mitigation measures are in place
- Instructions for use and labelling
- Statement of compliance with **ISO 14155** and MDR GCP requirements
- Prior submission history — including any refusals in other Member States

**German additions the EC will specifically police:**
- **Subject insurance (Probandenversicherung).** This is a hard national requirement and a common reason for a hold. There is a statutory minimum sum per subject — my recollection is €500,000, carried over from the old MPG; confirm the current figure and the exact MPDG § before binding cover.
- **Patient information and informed consent forms in German**, and separate GDPR/BDSG data-processing consent. ECs here scrutinise the data-protection text closely — separate consent for data and, if applicable, biosample use.
- **Investigator qualification**: CVs, GCP/ISO 14155 training records, and the investigator declaration. For a Class III implant, expect the EC to test whether the investigators' clinical experience matches the device.
- **Site suitability** declarations, including emergency/ICU backup appropriate to the risk class.
- **Contracts**: site agreements, investigator remuneration, funding disclosure — ECs review these for undue inducement.
- **Recruitment material** in final form.
- **Vulnerable-population justification** where relevant. MPDG's rules on minors and adults lacking capacity are *stricter* than the MDR baseline — if your Class III study touches these groups, treat this as a distinct workstream and get the exact §§ confirmed early.
- **Radiation protection**: if the investigation involves ionising radiation, that's a *separate* authorisation track under the Strahlenschutzgesetz with its own EC involvement and its own clock. Don't let it discover you late.

| Step | Clock |
|---|---|

| Your window to comment/complete if it's deficient | **max 10 days**; miss it and the application **lapses** |

- **Requests for additional information suspend the 45-day clock** — from the date of the request until the response is received. In practice this is where most of the calendar goes. Assume a request for information (RFI) rather than hoping for a clean pass, and pre-build the response capacity.

## Which regime applies

An unapproved (non-CE-marked) Class III device studied to demonstrate conformity falls under **Art. 62 MDR (EU) 2017/745**, implemented nationally by the **MPDG** (in force 26 May 2021), Chapter 4. This is *not* the lighter "sonstige klinische Prüfung" regime (Art. 82 MDR / MPDG §§ 47 ff.).

Germany requires **two independent decisions** before you may start:

1. **Authorisation (Genehmigung)** by the Bundesoberbehörde — **BfArM**, or **PEI** if the device incorporates or is used with blood/plasma/tissue derivatives.
2. **Favourable opinion (zustimmende Bewertung)** of a **registered ethics committee** — one formed under Länder law *and* registered with BfArM. You cannot use an arbitrary local EK; BfArM publishes the register.

Both are triggered by a **single electronic submission via DMIDS**, which routes the dossier to the BOB and the EK in parallel. Get your **Single Identification Number (SIN)** before submitting.

## Ethics committee dossier

The content is set by **Art. 62(4), 70(1) and Annex XV Chapter II MDR**, plus the German additions in MPDG:

**Core scientific documentation**
- Application form + SIN
- **Clinical Investigation Plan** (Annex XV Ch. II §3) — full statistical rationale, endpoints, risk/benefit analysis, subject withdrawal criteria
- **Investigator's Brochure**
- Technical documentation summary: design, manufacturing, **risk analysis and risk-mitigation measures**, biocompatibility, sterilisation/packaging validation, software V&V, bench and animal data
- **Declaration that the device conforms to the Annex I GSPRs** apart from the aspects under investigation, and that those aspects are covered by mitigation measures
- ISO 14155 conformity statement

**Subject-protection documentation (the EK's main focus)**
- Subject information sheet and **informed consent form, in German**
- **Insurance certificate (Probandenversicherung)** — MPDG requires per-subject cover; the figure usually cited is €500,000 per subject (worth confirming against the current text)
- Justification under MPDG's special provisions if you enrol **minors, adults lacking capacity, pregnant/nursing women, or in emergency situations** — these are stricter than the MDR baseline and are where German EKs most often push back
- GDPR/BDSG data-protection concept and separate data-processing consent; lay summary commitment
- Recruitment material, diaries, questionnaires

**Site and personnel**
- CVs and GCP/ISO 14155 training for each investigator; **suitability declarations for every site**
- Sponsor's EU establishment or **EU legal representative** (Art. 62(2))
- Financing, investigator contracts, subject compensation

**Easily missed:** if the protocol involves X-ray or radioactive substances, you additionally need a **StrlSchG § 31 approval from BfS** — a separate procedure with its own timeline that frequently becomes the critical path.

## Deadlines

| Step | Clock |
|---|---|
| **Validation** of the application | 10 days from receipt; if incomplete, sponsor has ≤10 days to complete, authority then 5 more days. Silence = deemed validated (Art. 70(1)–(3)) |
| **Decision on a Class III device** | **45 days from the validation date**, extendable by **+20 days** for expert consultation → **max. 65 days** (Art. 70(7)(b)) |
| Requests for information | Suspend the assessment clock |
| **Start of the investigation** | Only after **express notification of authorisation**. There is **no tacit approval** for Class III — unlike Class I / non-invasive IIa–IIb, which may start on the validation date |
| **Substantial modification** | Implement no earlier than **38 days** after notification, absent objection — and a favourable EK assessment of the change is required (Art. 75) |
| **SAE / device deficiency reporting** | **2 calendar days** where the event indicates imminent risk of death or serious deterioration requiring prompt remedial action; **7 calendar days** otherwise (Art. 80 + MDCG 2020-10/1) |
| **Temporary halt or early termination** | 15 days; **24 hours** if on safety grounds (Art. 77(2)) |
| **End of investigation** | 15 days per Member State (Art. 77(1), (3)) |
| **Clinical investigation report** | **1 year** after end of investigation, or **3 months** after early termination/halt (Art. 77(5)) |

- **Budget from submission, not from validation.** Worst case for Class III is 10 + 65 days plus any clock stops for information requests; a single round of EK questions realistically puts you at 3–4 months to green light.
- **Länder authorities** are informed of your sites and are the GCP inspection body — separate from the EK, and relevant to site readiness rather than to the submission itself.

| Step | Clock | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Validation (in scope + complete) | **10 days** from receipt; silence = deemed validated | MDR Art. 70(1) |
| Your response if declared incomplete | **max 10 days**, else application lapses; authority then 5 days to validate | MDR Art. 70(1) |
| Assessment → authorise / refuse / still assessing | **45 days from the validation date** | MDR Art. 70(7) |
| Extension for expert consultation | **+20 days** (→ 65 days) | MDR Art. 70(7) |
| Substantial modification | notify; implement **no earlier than 38 days** after notification absent objection | MDR Art. 75(3) |
| SAE / serious device deficiency — imminent risk of death or serious injury requiring prompt remedial action | **immediately, ≤ 2 calendar days** | MDR Art. 80; MDCG 2020-10 |
| Other reportable SAEs / device deficiencies | **≤ 7 calendar days** | same |
| Halt on safety grounds | **24 hours** | MDR Art. 77 |
| End of investigation / early termination notification | **15 days** | MDR Art. 77 |
| Clinical investigation report | **1 year** after end; **3 months** after early termination | MDR Art. 77(5) |

Realistic submission-to-first-patient for a Class III device: **3–4 months**, longer if radiation is involved (below).

## Dossier for the ethics committee

Annex XV Chapter II core:

1. Signed application form; single identification number.
2. **Investigator's Brochure.**
3. **Clinical Investigation Plan** per Annex XV Ch. II §3 — endpoints, statistics and sample-size justification, risk mitigation, monitoring plan, data-management plan, stopping rules, DSMB if applicable.
4. **GSPR statement** — which Annex I requirements are met, which are the subject of the investigation, and the justification.
5. **Benefit-risk analysis** and risk management file (ISO 14971).
6. **Pre-clinical evidence package**: bench/performance testing, biocompatibility (ISO 10993), electrical safety and EMC (IEC 60601 series), sterilisation and packaging validation, software verification and validation (IEC 62304) plus cybersecurity where relevant, animal data, and the clinical evaluation/literature per Annex XIV Part A. 7. Device description, manufacturing information, and labelling bearing **"exclusively for clinical investigation"**.
8. **Subject information and informed consent form — in German**, lay-level; separate GDPR information.
9. Suitability of sites and qualification of investigators (CVs, facilities, infrastructure).
10. Data protection concept (GDPR + relevant Land data protection law), pseudonymisation, retention, transfers.
11. **Financial arrangements**: site/investigator compensation, subject compensation and travel costs, funding source, conflict-of-interest declarations, recruitment procedures and any advertising material.
12. Signed sponsor statement that the device conforms to the GSPRs apart from the aspects under investigation.

- **Probandenversicherung** — subject insurance certificate is a hard precondition; MPDG sets a statutory minimum sum per subject (I believe €500,000 — confirm the figure and that the policy covers all German sites and the full follow-up period).
- **Investigator qualification** — MPDG imposes a minimum experience requirement on the Prüfer (on the order of two years' clinical-investigation experience); the EC will reject CVs that don't evidence it.

- **Ionising radiation for research purposes** triggers a *separate* approval under **§ 31 StrlSchG** (or notification under § 32) from the Bundesamt für Strahlenschutz, with a favourable EC opinion as a prerequisite. - **Drug-device combinations or devices with a medicinal substance** can pull in AMG requirements and change which authority leads. Settle the regulatory qualification before you file.

**German market:** confirmed — devices affected in Germany

| Item | MDR requires | Germany adds | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| FSN language | not carried here (MDR Art. 89(8) requires an FSN; language is left to member states) `[verify]` | FSN **must be written in German** where a manufacturer takes an FSCA within Germany | MPDG § 73(1) `[verified]` |
| Does US establishment excuse it? | — | No. § 73(1) attaches to the **action** taken *im Geltungsbereich dieses Gesetzes*, not to the manufacturer's seat | MPDG § 73(1) `[verified]` |
| Document FSCA + periodically review effectiveness | not carried here | Required — but only for manufacturers **established in Germany**. You are US-established, so this sentence does not bind you | MPDG § 73(2) s.1 `[verified]` |
| Notify **completion** of the FSCA to the competent authority *and* the federal higher authority | not carried here | Required of manufacturers, authorised representatives and importers **established in Germany**. 1. Produce a German-language version of the FSN before it goes to German recipients. Note this is separate from the § 8 language rules — there is no professional-user exception in § 73(1) at all, so "it only goes to clinicians" doesn't help here. 2. Tell your German importer(s) about their § 73(2) completion-notification duty. Because your AR is Irish rather than German, that duty lands on them, and importers frequently don't know it exists. You'll want the FSCA closure evidence flowing back to them.

**What would change this:** if Germany were not actually in scope — devices not made available there and no FSCA action there — § 73(1) would not apply. Nothing about your US establishment or Irish AR changes the German FSN language requirement.

**On the other affected countries:** I can't help you there. Each member state has its own MDR implementing act with its own FSN language rules, and several will require the national language too.
